title: The Useless Vine
summary: In a short parable, God asks what the wood of a vine is good for. It cannot be made into furniture or even a peg; it is fit only for fuel, and once burned at both ends and charred in the middle it is worth even less. So the people of Jerusalem, already scorched by one fire, will be given to another, and the land will be made desolate because they have acted unfaithfully.
story: Chapter 15 is the first of several parables and allegories in chapters 15 to 17, each of which pictures Jerusalem in a new image: a vine (chapter 15), an unfaithful wife (chapter 16), and a cedar and a vine caught between two eagles (chapter 17). Together they take on the pride of a city that believed its status as God's chosen people guaranteed its survival. Chapter 14 had just ruled out the hope that a few righteous people could save the city. This chapter answers a different hope: that Israel, as God's vine, was too valuable to be destroyed. The vine had been one of Israel's cherished pictures of itself. Ezekiel turns it upside down.
historical: The oracle is undated but belongs to the years before the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Verse 7 speaks of people who “escaped the fire” only to face another fire. This most likely refers to the deportation of 597 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, carried off King Jehoiachin, the leading families, and the temple treasures, but left the city standing. Those who remained in Jerusalem saw themselves as survivors and perhaps as the favored ones (compare 11:15). Ezekiel's picture says that the city has been burned at both ends and charred in the middle already, and the next fire will finish it. Some interpreters also see an allusion to the earlier losses Judah had suffered, such as the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC, but the 597 BC deportation is the nearest and clearest reference.
cultural:
Grapevines were among the most important crops of ancient Israel, alongside grain and olives. Vineyards covered the hill country, and wine was part of daily life and of Israel's feasts. Because of that importance, the vine became a common image for Israel itself. Psalm 80 describes Israel as a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted, and Isaiah 5 tells the song of a vineyard that produced only bad grapes. Hosea 10:1 calls Israel a luxuriant vine. The people of Jerusalem would have heard the image with pride: they were God's vine, carefully planted and tended.

Ezekiel's audience would also know that the value of a vine is entirely in its fruit. Unlike oak or cedar, vine wood is soft, twisted, and thin. It cannot be used for building, furniture, or tools, and it is too weak even for a peg on which to hang a pot. Pruned branches were gathered and burned, as Jesus also noted (John 15:6). Ezekiel quietly leaves out the fruit altogether: he speaks only of the wood. A vine that yields no fruit has no other use.
literary: The chapter is a brief parable in two parts: the picture (verses 1 to 5) and its application (verses 6 to 8). The picture proceeds through a series of rhetorical questions, each expecting the answer no: does the vine's wood surpass other trees, can it be used for anything, can it even make a peg? The questions draw the hearer into agreeing before the application is made. The argument moves from lesser to greater in verse 5: if the wood was useless whole, how much less once burned. The application then repeats key words from the picture, the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest and the fire, and ends with the recognition formula and a closing charge of unfaithfulness.

outline.t: The parable: what is vine wood good for
The application: Jerusalem given to the fire

doctrines.note: Judgment comes to Jerusalem “because they have acted unfaithfully” (verse 8). Israel's privilege as God's vine does not exempt it; it makes its lack of fruit all the more serious.

Israel's value lay not in itself but in its relationship with God and its calling to bear the fruit of faithfulness. The covenant was a calling to be fruitful, not a guarantee of safety regardless of faithfulness.

The parable puts human pride in its place. Israel was chosen not because of its natural strength, but for a purpose. Apart from that purpose, it had no greater worth than any other people, a humbling reminder for anyone who presumes on God's favor.

words.note: Gefen, vine. The word usually refers to the grapevine, and it became one of the richest symbols of Israel in the Old Testament. Ezekiel returns to the image in 17:6-8 and 19:10-14. Here he deliberately strips the symbol of its pride by talking only about its wood.

Melakhah, work or craftsmanship. It appears four times in this short chapter in the question of whether the vine's wood can be made into anything useful. The same word describes God's work of creation in Genesis 2:2 and the skilled work of building the tabernacle. Vine wood has no place in any such work.

Ma'al, unfaithfulness or treachery. It is a strong word used for breaking faith with God, especially by taking what belongs to him or turning to other gods. It closes the chapter (verse 8) and names the reason the vine is burned: not merely fruitlessness but betrayal.

christ: Jesus took up the image of the vine and applied it to himself: “I am the true vine,” he said, and his Father is the vinedresser (John 15:1). He told his disciples that a branch that does not remain in him is thrown away and withers, and such branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned (John 15:6), language very close to this chapter. The difference is where the vine's life is found. Israel, as the vine, had failed to bear fruit; Jesus presents himself as the true vine, and those who remain in him bear much fruit. The connection is explicit in the image, though John 15 does not quote Ezekiel directly.

hard.q: Is it fair to call God's people useless, as if their only value were their productivity?
hard.a: The parable is blunt, and readers who have been told they were worthless may hear it painfully. It helps to see what the image is aimed at. Ezekiel speaks to a proud city that believed its chosen status made it safe no matter what it did. The point is not that people are valuable only for what they produce, but that Israel's special standing rested on its calling to be faithful, and that calling had been abandoned. Elsewhere Ezekiel insists that God takes no pleasure in the death of anyone (18:32) and promises a new heart and a restored people (chapters 11, 36, 37). The parable humbles pride; it does not describe how God sees every human being. If you have been told you are worthless, the Bible's wider witness is that every person bears the image of God and is loved by him.

questions: The people of Jerusalem took pride in being God's vine. Where are you tempted to rely on your status or identity rather than on faithfulness?
Ezekiel speaks only of the vine's wood and never of its fruit. What would it mean for your life to bear fruit?
How does Jesus' claim to be the true vine change the way you read this chapter?
